newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-VEGAS PARKING LOT VENUE FOR BAILEY-JOHNSON RE-MATCH ?.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-VEGAS PARKING LOT VENUE FOR BAILEY-JOHNSON RE-MATCH ?.

text.p: Olympic sprint champions Donovan Bailey and Michael Johnson, who clashed in an anti-climatic $1.5 million showdown a month ago, could meet each other in a rematch later this year in a Las Vegas parking lot.

Although the idea surfaced soon after Bailey beat Johnson in Toronto on May 31 and appeared then to be a non-starter, Bailey's manager Ray Flynn said on Friday he was "totally serious" about the idea.
"There has been a great deal of interest shown in a rematch and I think the people supporting Michael Johnson would be very keen on another race as their man did not do himself justice in Toronto.

"You can lay a Mondo strip of track anywhere and if the money was right, a parking lot at one of the big Las Vegas hotels could be the ideal place to stage the race. I am totally serious about this. The race could take place anywehere. Why not there?

"I think any rematch should be over 150 metres again. You could either have a straight race, or a 150 with one turn as we had in Toronto. But whatever the venue, I think the chances of a rematch somewhere in North America are very high."

Championship boxing matches have been held in converted Las Vegas parking lots for years and other sporting events such as a Formula One Grand Prix have also been held in the American gambling capital deep in the Nevada desert.
Another head-to-head to try and establish the world's fastest man would certainly appear to the gambling instincts of Vegas's high-rollers.
Bailey, who picked up $1.0 million in prize money and another $500,000 appearance fee in Toronto, won after the American pulled up with an injury 50 metres from the line.
The Canadian was extremely critical of his opponent afterwards, calling him "a chicken" and doubting the extent of his injury. But on Friday he was contrite.
"I said things I should not have said afterwards," he said.
"But I was reacting just minutes after the race and a lot of comments had been made by Michael before the race. I was never taught to beat around the bush and said exactly what I thought.
"I would be interested if the package was right but, unlike in Toronto, I would rather any race was staged in an athletics environment. But we'll have to wait and see."
Another compelling argument for a rematch was the TV audience for the race in Toronto which Flynn said was "a huge green light to potential sponsors."

The race had a huge audience in Canadian television terms with 3.6 million viewiers or about one in nine of the population. It was a higher viewership than the 3.4 million who watched Bailey win the Olympic 100 metres last year in Atlanta.

"That represented very cheap programming for the TV companies and I know they would be interested in another race. I think certain other safeguards would have to be built into any rematch in case one of the runners was injured as happened in Toronto, but I am sure it will happen later this year."
Any rematch would need to be sanctioned by the International Amateur Arthletic Federation whose president Primo Nebiolo is reported to be highly critical of the "circus elements" of similiar events.
